li.a: LawFuel, 9 May 2007: former NSW crown prosecutor sentenced to 15 months' jail on child porn charges
Lawyers Weekly, 21 June 2007: Power 'addicted to child porn'
NSW Caselaw: Police v Power, sentencing judgment
Sydney Morning Herald, 25 May 2007: Newspaper subjected lawyers to scurrilous abuse, court told
ABC News (archived), 18 January 2008: Top prosecutor Power 'sorry' for child porn

content.p: Patrick Power built a long career inside the New South Wales justice system. He practised at the state's Bar from 1986, became a Crown Prosecutor the following year and a Deputy Senior Crown Prosecutor in 1991, and was later appointed Senior Counsel. In 2007 he pleaded guilty to possessing child pornography. The case drew attention for its material and for what came after it: a dispute between the Bar Association and a Sydney newspaper over the people who had written character references for him.
content.h2: A prosecutor with a long career
content.p: The NSW sentencing judgment, published on the state's Caselaw database under the name Police v Power, sets out his professional history. It records that he held a Bachelor of Laws, a Master of Laws and a Doctorate. The judge described him as "a highly intelligent man", noting that many of his referees said so. The judgment also records that the Bar had recognised his competence by appointing him Senior Counsel.
On that point the judgment was direct: the judge said that, unlike other members of the community, Power was "uniquely placed to understand the nature of his conduct".
content.h2: What was found on the computer
content.p: According to LawFuel, investigators uncovered almost 29,000 images on the hard drive of Power's personal computer. Most of them were homosexual pornography. However, 433 of the images showed children, and LawFuel said some of those children were under 10. A separate set of 31 videos, according to the same report, showed adults engaged in sex acts with children. LawFuel reported that a court heard the material had been collected over several years, while Power worked as one of the state's top prosecutors.

The ABC reported that Power had handed the computer to the office of the Director of Public Prosecutions for repair. Lawyers Weekly said the material was discovered during routine maintenance. The two reports date different events. Lawyers Weekly, writing in June 2007, said the material was found "last year". The ABC, writing in January 2008, said Power was arrested and charged "last year".

The sentencing judgment dealt with a specific question about concealment. The judge said the files had been hidden in folders named "Quicken" and "Thesis backup". The judge rejected the defence submission that the files had reached those folders at random, saying the "overwhelming inference" was that they had been placed there deliberately, knowing what they were.

Power pleaded guilty in January 2007, according to Lawyers Weekly. He was sentenced in May 2007 at the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney, where LawFuel said he received 15 months' jail and was granted bail pending an appeal against that sentence. Lawyers Weekly gave a non-parole period of at least eight months. The judgment set the non-parole period at eight months within a total term of fifteen months, to commence forthwith.

The judgment shows how the sentence was reached. The judge set the appropriate sentence at 18 months, applied a discount of 16.5 per cent for the guilty plea, and arrived at 15 months. The judge described the offence as lying "towards the middle of the range" of offences of this type. The judge considered suspending the sentence and then found special circumstances, based on hardship, to vary the usual link between the minimum period and the head sentence. The Department of Corrective Services had acknowledged that the nature of his profession created a genuine risk to his safety, and that he would need protective custody. The judge accepted that assessment, while adding that hardship was not in itself a reason to avoid prison.
On the mental condition relied on by the defence, the judge concluded that general deterrence remained, in the judge's words, "not just significant, but a paramount consideration."
The ABC reported a later figure. In July 2007, it said, the District Court reduced his non-parole period to six months. Only the ABC reports that reduction.

At the hearing for a reduced sentence, Power's counsel, Philip Bolten, argued that his client had suffered from chronic depression since the 1970s. Bolten argued that the lower court had accepted a series of psychiatric evaluations but had disregarded their substantive weight because Power was a senior lawyer for the Crown, as Lawyers Weekly reported. Bolten said his client was not able to put a stop to the habit of downloading pornography from the internet. He told the court that Power had been "coping at work, doing his job as best he could" while the rest of his life was in "serious disarray".

Lawyers Weekly quoted Bolten as saying that Power was addicted to child pornography. That is the defence's account. The judge agreed with the prosecution's submissions on the psychiatric report. The judge rejected the defence submission that the material had reached the hidden folders randomly.
content.h2: The character referees and the Daily Telegraph
content.p: Several people wrote character references for Power. LawFuel reported that the Daily Telegraph published the names of 59 referees under the headline "Pervert and his 59 mates". The referees included defence barristers and prosecutors, along with family and friends.

The NSW Bar Association took legal action in response. Its president, Michael Slattery, told reporters outside the Downing Centre that the proceeding did not object to the referees being named. He argued that the headline and story put the administration of justice at risk, and said they could amount to defamation. The Association applied for the paper's publisher, News Ltd, to be charged with contempt of court.

In court, the Association's barrister, Bret Walker SC, argued that the referees had been "vilified" and "humiliated". He said the Telegraph and the Sunday Telegraph had failed to say that the referees did not condone Power's crimes. He also said the paper had acted like a "self-appointed guardian" of the law. Walker argued that every offender had the right to call character references, and that anything which deterred referees from coming forward "strikes at the heart of the administration of justice".

The ABC reported in January 2008 that Power was released from Sydney's Long Bay jail that morning. He had served six months, and he told reporters the time had been very difficult. "I've been held in complete isolation," he said. In a statement on his release, he said he deeply regretted his "inappropriate behaviour" and apologised to his family, friends and former colleagues.

The ABC also recorded that the sentencing judge had described the contents of the computer as "disgusting" and "depraved". The NSW Bar Association later stripped Power of his right to practise. A spokesman said he had no practising certificate and that a hearing was planned for May 2008 before the NSW Court of Appeal to have him permanently disbarred. The ABC reported that he had also been placed on the state's list of sex offenders.

Two points stay open. The judgment and Lawyers Weekly both give a non-parole period of eight months, while only the ABC reports a reduction to six months. And the outcome of the planned 2008 disbarment hearing, and of the appeal LawFuel mentioned, is not reported in the cited pages.
